claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is initially a high-temperature BCC phase.
The stability of the high-temperature BCC phase in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is governed by the degree of short-range chemical ordering.
The relevant short-range ordering occurs between Al and neighboring Cr/Ni atoms.
Insufficient chemical ordering at high temperature maintains the disordered BCC structure.
Cooling increases diffusion and thereby promotes local Al–(Cr/Ni) clustering.
High thermal kinetic energy prevents significant atomic ordering.
Slow cooling permits sufficient diffusion for local Al–(Cr/Ni) ordering to develop.
Local Al–(Cr/Ni) ordering lowers the free energy of the alloy.
The free-energy reduction caused by ordering drives transformation from disordered BCC toward ordered B2.
Rapid cooling kinetically suppresses ordering and preserves the disordered BCC state.
Slow cooling will produce emerging and growing diffraction peaks characteristic of ordered B2.
The B2 diffraction peaks constitute evidence of the proposed short-range ordering.
Rapidly cooled samples will retain BCC with minimal evidence of ordering.
Cooling rate will correlate with the intensity or fraction of ordered features.
A rapidly quenched sample can serve as a reference in which ordering effects are absent.
The proposed mechanism operates only in a temperature interval where diffusion is appreciable but thermal disorder does not dominate.
There is a critical cooling-rate threshold controlling whether ordering develops.
Short-range order can alter relative phase stability through composition-dependent local energetics.

contradictions.description: The mediator is defined as short-range order or local clustering, whereas the predicted readout is the appearance of B2 phase peaks, which ordinarily evidences long-range ordered periodicity rather than directly measuring short-range order.

The prediction treats slower cooling as favoring ordering, but the boundary states that effects may disappear when cooling rate falls below a critical threshold, without explaining why still slower cooling would reverse or suppress ordering.
